title: Statistical Disorder in MBE-Grown AlGaAs/GaAs Superlattices for Quantum Bragg Mirrors using Synchrotron X-ray Diffraction
authors: Mateus T. Souza, Germano M. Penello, Guilherme A. Calligaris, Sergio L. Morelhao
abstract: AlGaAs/GaAs superlattices grown by Molecular Beam Epitaxy (MBE) are foundational for advanced optoelectronic devices, including Quantum Bragg Mirror (QBM) infrared detectors. The performance of these devices critically depends on achieving near-perfect periodicity and abrupt interfaces, however, intrinsic statistical fluctuations during MBE growth introduce nanoscale structural disorder that can degrade device efficiency. In this study, we present a comprehensive methodology for quantifying this disorder in a 203-layer QBM device. High-resolution structural characterization was performed using high-energy (25 keV) synchrotron X-ray diffraction. By coupling a recursive dynamical diffraction formalism with an ensemble simulated annealing refinement, we extracted statistically robust, layer-by-layer thickness profiles. Our analysis reveals highly systematic, material-specific deviations from the nominal design: all AlGaAs barrier layers were consistently thinner than nominal by 0.3-0.6 nm. Furthermore, the sequential thickness profile successfully identified a significant 35 nm deficit in the final macroscopic top contact layer and a 40 nm deficit in the first GaAs layer. Achieving a statistical precision of about 0.2 to 0.6 nm (approximately 1-2 atomic monolayers), this non-destructive diagnostic approach provides directly actionable feedback for MBE flux calibration protocols.
summary: This work uses high-energy synchrotron X-ray diffraction combined with simulated annealing to precisely map the layer-by-layer structure of an AlGaAs/GaAs superlattice QBM. The analysis successfully quantified systematic growth errors, such as consistent thinning of barrier layers, providing critical, non-destructive feedback to improve the Molecular Beam Epitaxy growth process for high-performance quantum devices.
main_problem: The study aims to quantify nanoscale structural disorder in AlGaAs/GaAs superlattices used in Quantum Bragg Mirror (QBM) infrared detectors.
main_result: The analysis revealed systematic, material-specific thinning of AlGaAs barrier layers (0.3-0.6 nm) and significant deficits in the top and bottom contact layers, providing actionable feedback for MBE flux calibration.
method: High-resolution structural characterization was performed using synchrotron X-ray diffraction, coupled with a recursive dynamical diffraction formalism and ensemble simulated annealing refinement.
model_or_system: The physical system is a 203-layer AlGaAs/GaAs superlattice designed as a QBM. The analysis models the structural periodicity and composition to match experimental X-ray reflectivity data.
key_observables: Layer-by-layer thickness profiles, structural parameters ($ ar{X}$), and the $\chi^2$ cost function value comparing simulated vs. experimental reflectivity.
important_parameters: Synchrotron X-ray energy (25 keV); diagnostic precision of 0.2 to 0.6 nm (1-2 atomic monolayers); systematic thickness deficits (e.g., 35 nm, 40 nm).
main_assumptions: The method assumes that structural disorder can be quantified by fitting the X-ray reflectivity curve, and the optimization is heavily weighted towards reproducing peak positions.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the schematic of the nominal heterostructure. Figure 2 compares experimental and simulated X-ray reflectivity curves (Refined vs. Nominal). Figure 3 details the thickness profile within the active region.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the need to quantify disorder, details the methodology combining dynamical diffraction theory with simulated annealing optimization, presents the systematic analysis of the 203-layer structure, and concludes with actionable feedback for improving MBE growth protocols.
why_interesting: While the core physics is solid-state characterization, the rigorous application of advanced numerical optimization (SA) to extract precise, actionable structural parameters from complex scattering data is valuable for understanding material limitations in quantum devices.
